## Background

Today we will explore some core machine learning methods that are very popular in bioinformatics. These include **clustering** and **dimensionallity reduction**.

## K-means

The main function "base R" for k-means clustering is called `kmeans()`


Before we go too deep let's make up some "simple" data that we can cluster and know if we are getting good results or not.

```{r}
hist(rnorm(100000))
```

Give me 30 points centered at -3 and a second set with a mean of +3

```{r} 
tmp <- c( rnorm(30, mean=-3), rnorm(30, mean=+3))

x <- cbind(x = tmp, y = rev(tmp))
x


```

```{r}
plot(x)
```


Now try `kmean()` on this input data` x`

```{r}
k <- kmeans(x, centers = 2)
k
```

To get to the results we can use `k$size` etc. to access each compnent results:


> Q. How many points are in each cluster?

```{r}
k$size
```

> Q. What "compnent" of your results object details cluster membership?

```{r}
k$cluster
```




> Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster centers?


```{r}
k$centers
```


> Q. Make a results figure of our data with points colored by cluster along with cluster centers?

```{r}
plot(x, col=c(1,2))
```

```{r}
plot(x, col=k$cluster)
points(k$centers, col="blue", pch=15)
```

> Q. Run kmeans again and cluster into 4 cluster producing a result figure with points colored ny cluster and showing the cluser centers?

```{r}
km <- kmeans(x, centers = 4)
plot(x, col=k$cluster)
points(k$centers, col="blue", pch=15)
```

> **N.B** You need to tell k-means the number of clusters (i.e. set `centers=2`)!!

One approach is to try different values for `centers` and then pick the best one:


```{r}
ans <- NULL

for(i in 1:10) {
  #cat(i, "\n")
km <- kmeans(x, centers = 4)
ans <- c(ans, km$tot.withinss)
}
```


```{r}
plot(ans, type="o",
     xlab="Number of cluster",
     ylab="Total sum of Squares Distance")
```


## Hierarchical Clustering

The main function in "base" R for is called `hclust()`

This function does not take your "row" data for clustering, You must first build a "distance matric" from your data and pass this as input for `hclust`.

```{r}
d <- dist(x)

hc <- hclust(d)
hc
```

```{r}
plot(hc)
abline(h=8, col="red")
```


Once sd have our `hclust` object (our "tree" or "cluster denrogram") we can "cut" the tree to reveal the clustering pattern:

```{r}
cutree(hc, h=8)
```


You can use either `h=` or `k=` arfuments to `cutree()`

```{r}
cutree(hc, k=4)
```


> Q. Make a plot of input data `x` with your clusters from `hclust` (i.e. colored by cluster membership fro cutting the tree)? 

```{r}
cutree(hc, h=8)
```


You can use either `h=` or `k=` arguments to `cutree()`

```{r}
cutree(hc, k=4)
```


> Q. Make a plot of input data `x` with your clusters from `hclust` (i.e. colored by cluster membership fro cutting the tree)? 


```{r}
cutree(hc, h=8)
```


You can use either `h=` or `k=` arfuments to `cutree()`

```{r}
cutree(hc, k=4)
```


> Q. Make a plot of input data `x` with your clusters from `hclust` (i.e. colored by cluster membership fro cutting the tree)? 



```{r}
grps <- cutree(hc, h=8)
plot(x, col=grps)
```

## Princple Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is a dimensionality reduction method that is poplular for revealing patterns in complex dataset.


### Analysis of UK food data

Let's look at some data on eating habits of folks from the UK to see if there are patterns and trends that have some regions being distinct form others.


### Data import

The data is made available in CSV format so we can use `read.csv()` :

```{r}
x <- read.csv("https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods", row.names = 1)
x
```

> Q1. How many rows and columns are in your new data frame named x?

```{r}
nrow(x)
ncol(x)
```

> Q2. Which approach to solving the ‘row-names problem’ mentioned above do you prefer and why? Is one approach more robust than another under certain circumstances?

To solve the 'row-names problem' I used the code `row.names = 1`. I preferred this method because it allowed us to solve our problem with a simple short code. The code I used is also more accurate because if we use the second method `rownames(x) <- x[,1]x <- x[,-1] head(x)` and run it multiple times the code can delete more columns in our data.


Some plots:

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=T, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```


> Q3. Changing what optional argument in the above barplot() function results in the following plot?

- I only changed the `beside= T` code to `beside=F`. This changed the bars from side to side to stacked.

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=F, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```


> Q4: Changing what optional argument in the above ggplot() code results in a stacked barplot figure?

Original plot:

```{r}

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

x_long <- x |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Food") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -Food,
    names_to = "Country",
    values_to = "Consumption"
  )

ggplot(x_long) +
  aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  theme_bw()
```



```{r}
ggplot(x_long) +
  aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  theme_bw()
```
I only changed my argument in position from "dodge" to "stack", which changes my plot from side by side bar plot to a stacked barplot.


### Pairs plots and heatmaps


One plot that can be useful for relatively small datasets is a `pairs()` plot:


```{r}
pairs(x, col=rainbow(nrow(x)), pch=16)
```

> Q5: We can use the pairs() function to generate all pairwise plots for our countries. Can you make sense of the following code and resulting figure? What does it mean if a given point lies on the diagonal for a given plot?

- Our pairs argument will compare the food consumption between the different countries in our data. And each point on the plot will show a food category, for example if we  have a point that lies diagonally on the plot that means that both countries on the plot are sharing the same consumption amount for that food category.


> Q6. Based on the pairs and heatmap figures, which countries cluster together and what does this suggest about their food consumption patterns? Can you easily tell what the main differences between N. Ireland and the other countries of the UK in terms of this data-set?

- After analyzing our heat map we can conclude that the countries England, Scotland, Wales cluster together, this is because they have similar food consumption trends. We can also see that the country Northern Ireland has  different food consumption than the other countries. We can see that Northern Ireland consumes fresh potatoes more and they eat less fruits than other countries. 


> **Key-point**: Even relatively small datasets can prove challenging to interpret 


Given that it is quite difficult to make sense of even this relatively small data set. Hopefully, we can clearly see that a powerful analytical method is absolutely necessary if we wish to observe trends and patterns in larger datasets.

## PCA to the rescue!


The main function in "base" R  for PCA is called `prcomp()`:

This function will require the transpose fo our datset - 

```{r}
pca <- prcomp( t(x))
```

We cna see how well our PCA resutls are doing in terms of **variance captured** from the original data in each PC.

```{r}
summary(pca)
```

I can see what is in my `pca` result object by:
```{r}
attributes(pca)
```

Of these `pca$x` is our main result. WE can use it to make a result figure ogten called a PCA plot (or score-plot).

```{r}
pca$x
```
> Q7. Complete the code below to generate a plot of PC1 vs PC2. The second line adds text labels over the data points.

```{r}

x <- read.csv("https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods", row.names = 1)

pca <- prcomp(t(x))

df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = Country) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```


> Q8. Customize your plot so that the colors of the country names match the colors in our UK and Ireland map and table at start of this document.

```{r} 
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = Country, color = Country) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "England" = "orange",
    "Wales" = "red",
    "Scotland" = "blue",
    "N.Ireland" = "darkgreen"
  )) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```

A "loading" plot can shpw us the original dimension/variables contribute to our new PC axis. This is detailed in the  `pca$rotation` component of our result object:

```{r}
pca$rotation
```

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1 , row.names(pca$rotation)) +
  geom_col()
```


> Q9: Generate a similar ‘loadings plot’ for PC2. What two food groups feature prominantely and what does PC2 maninly tell us about?

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(x = PC2,
      y = reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC2)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("PC2 Loading Score") +
  ylab("") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```
- The two food groups that featureprominantely are soft drinks and fresh potato, and PC2 will help show the differences and trends of food consumption in different countries.



>Q10: How many genes and samples are in this data set? How many PCs do you think it will take to have a useful overview of this data set (see below)?

First we will read our data:

```{r}
url2 <- "https://tinyurl.com/expression-CSV"
rna.data <- read.csv(url2, row.names=1)
head(rna.data)
```

```{r}
nrow(rna.data)
ncol(rna.data)
```

```{r}
pca <- prcomp(t(rna.data), scale = TRUE)

summary(pca)
```

- The data set we read had 100 genes and 10 samples. After analyzing the data I think that 2 principle components are good enough to give us an overview of the data set, because looking at the data above we can see that PC1 and PC2 make up 94.9 percent of the variance in the data.
